questions.question: A square card is the whole. It is cut into 100 equal small squares, and 9 of those small squares are coloured. Which decimal tells how much of the card is coloured?
questions.explain: When the whole is split into 100 equal parts, each part is one hundredth, so 9 parts is 0.09 — the 9 sits in the hundredths place. The usual trap is writing 0.9, but that means 9 tenths, which would be 90 of the 100 small squares.

questions.question: A paper strip is the whole. It is cut into 10 equal pieces, and 5 of those pieces are coloured. Which decimal tells how much of the strip is coloured?
questions.explain: Ten equal parts means each part is one tenth, so 5 parts is 0.5 and the 5 goes in the first place after the point. Writing 0.05 is the common slip: that would mean 5 out of 100 equal parts, not 5 out of 10.

questions.question: A poster is the whole. It is divided into 100 equal parts, and 30 of those parts are painted blue. Which decimal shows the blue part of the poster?
questions.explain: 30 hundredths is the same as 3 tenths, so it is written 0.30 (or 0.3) with the 3 in the tenths place. Only 0.03 would mean 3 of the 100 parts, which is far less than 30 of them.

questions.question: A garden bed is the whole. It is divided into 100 equal squares, and 42 squares have seeds in them. The part with seeds is written as the decimal 0.42. Which digit is in the tenths place?
questions.explain: The first digit after the decimal point is the tenths place, so in 0.42 the 4 means 4 tenths (40 of the 100 squares) and the 2 means 2 hundredths. Many students grab the last digit, but 2 is in the hundredths place, not the tenths place.

questions.question: Nadia is writing numbers in her math notebook. How is the number six hundredths written as a decimal?
questions.explain: Hundredths is the second place after the decimal point, so six hundredths needs a 0 in the tenths place: 0.06. Writing 0.6 is the classic mix-up — that reads as six tenths, which is ten times bigger.

questions.question: A carton of milk at a Kelowna corner store costs $0.85. What does the digit 8 in $0.85 mean?
options: 8 hundredths of a dollar, which is 8 pennies
8 tenths of a dollar, which is 8 dimes
8 thousandths of a dollar
8 whole dollars
questions.explain: In money the first place after the point is tenths of a dollar (dimes) and the second is hundredths (pennies), so the 8 in $0.85 means 8 dimes and the 5 means 5 pennies. Calling the 8 ‘eight pennies’ is the common trap — that would only be $0.08.

questions.question: A ribbon in the art bin measures 0.7 m. Ms. Chan asks the class to write that same length using hundredths of a metre. Which one is correct?
questions.explain: Seven tenths fills 70 of the 100 equal hundredth-parts of a metre, so 0.7 m is written 0.70 m. Changing it to 0.07 m moves the 7 into the hundredths place and makes the ribbon ten times shorter.

questions.question: Which of these numbers has a 5 in the hundredths place?
questions.explain: Count the places after the point: first is tenths, second is hundredths, so 0.25 has 2 tenths and 5 hundredths. In 0.52 the 5 is in the tenths place, so seeing a 5 somewhere after the point is not enough — check which place it sits in.

questions.question: Liam colours 3 small squares on a card that is cut into 100 equal squares. He writes 0.3 and says, ‘There are 100 squares, so 0.3 means three hundredths.’ Which statement about Liam is correct?
options: Liam is right, because a card with 100 equal parts always makes hundredths, so 0.3 here means 3 of them.
Liam is wrong. 0.3 means three tenths, which would be 30 squares; three hundredths is written 0.03.
Liam is wrong. 0.3 means three ones, since the 3 counts whole squares; the point only separates it from the 0.
Liam is right. 0.3 means three hundredths, because the 3 stands for the 3 squares out of the 100 on the card.
questions.explain: The place a digit sits in decides its size: the first place after the point is tenths and the second is hundredths, so 3 of 100 squares is 0.03, not 0.3. The number of parts in the whole does not change the rule — you still have to put the 3 in the hundredths place.

questions.question: Priya empties her pocket at the school store in Burnaby and finds 3 dimes and 4 pennies. A dime is one tenth of a dollar and a penny is one hundredth of a dollar. How much money does she have, written as a decimal?
questions.explain: Dimes go in the tenths place and pennies go in the hundredths place, so 3 dimes and 4 pennies is $0.34. Swapping them to $0.43 puts the pennies in the tenths place and adds money Priya does not have.

questions.question: A Grade 4 class in Prince George measures new snow. On Monday they record 0.4 cm and on Tuesday they record 0.04 cm. Which statement is true?
options: Tuesday had more, because 0.04 has more digits after the point, and a longer decimal is a bigger amount.
Monday and Tuesday are equal, because both records use a 4 and a 0, and extra zeros never change a decimal.
Monday had more, because 0.4 is four tenths while 0.04 is only four hundredths, and a tenth beats a hundredth.
Tuesday had more, because four hundredths means 4 whole parts out of 10, and four tenths is only 4 out of 100.
questions.explain: Read each digit by its place: 0.4 is 4 tenths (40 hundredths) and 0.04 is only 4 hundredths, so Monday's snow is ten times deeper. Extra digits do not make a decimal bigger, and the same digit means different amounts in different places.

questions.question: On sports day, Ben's long jump is recorded as 2.08 m. Which statement about the digit 8 in 2.08 is correct?
options: The 8 is in the tenths place, so it means 8 tenths of a metre.
The 8 is in the hundredths place, so it means 8 tenths of a metre.
The 0 in the tenths place does nothing, so 2.08 m can also be written 2.8 m.
The 8 is in the hundredths place, so it means 8 hundredths of a metre.
questions.explain: After the decimal point the places go tenths, then hundredths, so in 2.08 the 0 holds the tenths place and the 8 means 8 hundredths of a metre. That 0 is a real placeholder — dropping it to make 2.8 m would move the 8 into the tenths place and stretch Ben's jump.
